title: How to get the most pizza for your money
description:
Same price: one 18-inch pizza or two 12-inch ones? Widths say two 12s (24 inches), but pizza is area: the 18-inch has 254 square inches, the two 12s only 226. Area grows with width times width (18 x 18 = 324, 12 x 12 x 2 = 288), so the single large is an eighth more food. Take an inch of crust off every edge and it gets better: 201 square inches of middle against 157, 28% more, because every extra pizza adds another rim. It's the same reason a 64-inch TV has 4 times the screen of a 32-inch one.

Numbers checked in code (exact areas and a 200,000-point Monte Carlo). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_a_circle

18x18 = 324, 2 x 12x12 = 288; ratio exactly 9/8 (an eighth more) (verify.py; Monte Carlo 200,000 points 1.123)

Same shape, double the diagonal -> 4x the area: 64-inch vs 32-inch TV (verify.py)

beats.say: You're ordering pizza for your friends, and the menu is about to trick you. Here's how you win.
Same price: one 18-inch pizza, or two 12-inch ones.
Two 12s make 24 inches of pizza. That looks like the deal. It isn't.
You eat area, not width. The 18-inch covers 254 square inches. Each 12-inch covers 113. Both together, 226.
Here's why. Area grows with width times width. 18 times 18 is 324. 12 times 12 is 144, and two of them make 288.
So the one big pizza is an eighth more food, for the same money.
Uh-oh. Your friend doesn't eat crust. Cut one inch off every edge.
The big one keeps 201 square inches of middle. The two small ones keep just 157. That's 28% more of the good part.
Every extra pizza adds another ring of crust. One big pizza has only one.
And there you have it: same money, more pizza, and way more cheese.
Area grows with the square of the width. It's why a 64-inch TV has 4 times the screen of a 32-inch one.
